sections.title: Does the "myth" description need more subtlety?

comments.author: Feline Hymnic
comments.text: In saying "" does this require more subtlety? Sure, Gen.1-11 is mythological, as discussed well in its "primeval history" article. That's basically fine. But Gen.12-50 has very different genre characteristics; indeed the word "myth" never appears in the main body of its "ancestral history" article. So isn't the statement about the whole book "" too blunt in not distinguishing the different genres across the primeval/ancestral divide? Note: I'm basing this on the summary in the article lead. But the myth-description in the main body (section "Genre") has the same over-generalisation problem, so it's probably better to start from there, then to reflect an appropriate summary back onto the lead.

comments.author: Remsense
comments.text: :Subtlety is nice, but I believe the passage in question adequately characterizes the whole text, as the purpose throughout both the primeval and ancestral history halves is to explain and interconnect the origins of the world and the Jewish people within it.

comments.author: Ancient Greek Scribe
comments.text: :That is incorrect, mainstream Biblical scholars primarily (as in not only, but mostly for the Book of Genesis' stories) consider the Genesis composition to be mythological and as etiology, not literal or historical. The Genesis creation narrative in particular is an origin myth that even draws on other ancient near-eastern traditions and cosmologies. You can read about the scholarly perspectives on that page in the Genesis creation narrative#Literal interpretations. Moreover, see Biblical literalism#Criticism by historical-critical methodology scholars.
